name: Libertarian Christianity
summary: Christian libertarianism combines Christian belief with libertarian politics: government is confined to restraining force, theft and fraud, individuals hold God-given rights, and other sins are for the church, family and conscience rather than the law. Welfare, education and the economy belong to voluntary and private action, not to the state, and the state is held to the same prohibition on initiating force as anyone else, which makes most adherents sharply critical of war and empire.
scope: The mainstream strand of explicitly Christian libertarian writing: Andrew Sandlin's 1996 essay 'The Christian Libertarian Idea' (maximum freedom under God's law), Jamin Hübner's 2018 academic introduction in the Christian Libertarian Review, and the public figures the Wikipedia article lists such as Ron Paul and Lord Acton. Sandlin's Reformed, theonomy-influenced version is more willing than most to list biblical crimes such as idolatry; the profile follows the common core and does not represent Christian anarchism or theonomic reconstructionism as such. Most answers on social and foreign issues are inferred from the core principles, since few texts address them directly.

furtherReading.title: Christian libertarianism (Wikipedia)
furtherReading.note: Short neutral overview of the idea and a list of figures associated with it.

furtherReading.title: The Christian Libertarian Idea (Andrew Sandlin, 1996)
furtherReading.note: The essay that popularised the label, arguing for the state as a limited ministry of justice.

furtherReading.title: Christian Libertarianism: An Introduction and Signposts for the Road Ahead (Jamin Hübner)
furtherReading.note: A long academic introduction covering non-aggression, decentralization, markets and open questions.

keyFigures.name: Ron Paul
keyFigures.role: American politician listed by the Wikipedia article as a Baptist Christian libertarian; cited by Hübner for opposing an empire that requires aggressive wars.

keyFigures.name: John Dalberg-Acton, 1st Baron Acton
keyFigures.role: Catholic historian listed by the Wikipedia article, quoted for the view that political liberty is the essential guardian of religious liberty.

sources.title: Christian libertarianism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Definition, limits of law to assault, theft and fraud, list of adherents, Acton on liberty.

sources.title: The Christian Libertarian Idea (repost of the 1996 essay)
sources.author: Andrew Sandlin
sources.usedFor: The state as a limited ministry of justice, no taxation for welfare, education or health, no economic regulation, church and state as separate spheres.

sources.title: Christian Libertarianism: An Introduction and Signposts for the Road Ahead
sources.author: Jamin Hübner, The Christian Libertarian Review 1 (2018)
sources.usedFor: Non-aggression applied to the state, war, conscription, decentralization, charity over welfare, markets, money and open internal debates.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Sandlin says the state may not tax citizens to fund health benefits; care belongs to church, family and voluntary associations.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Scripture gives magistrates no warrant to regulate the economy beyond honest weights and measures, so a wage floor is an unjustified coercive interference in contracts.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Hübner contrasts consumer sovereignty in free markets with state-run services that must be accepted however poor, and treats market exchange as voluntary and humane.

public-ownership.rationale: State-run industry rests on taxation and coercion and is outside the magistrate's biblical mandate; Hübner points to state services as unresponsive to the people they serve.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Sandlin denies the state any biblical task of redistributing wealth, so higher taxes on the rich for that purpose have no warrant.

unions-good.rationale: Voluntary association is welcome, but sources give no verdict on unions as good for society; Christian libertarians would defend the right to organize while rejecting compulsion and special privilege.

property-fundamental.rationale: Protection of property against theft is among the few legitimate functions of law, and Hübner treats eminent domain as land theft.

regulate-corporations.rationale: With no biblical warrant for state regulation of the economy, adherents oppose new regulatory powers; they dislike corporate privilege but would answer with law against fraud and force.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare is not a state function in Sandlin's account and Hübner says the poor need personal charity, not a welfare bureau, so cutting it follows; the dependency argument itself is less stressed.

worker-ownership.rationale: Voluntary cooperatives would be permitted but a collective-ownership programme is not part of the ideology; adherents would not endorse it as a goal.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Hübner applies non-aggression to the state like anyone else and treats state intrusion as the same wrong as a private actor's, so security does not license it.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Law is limited to assault, theft and fraud, with other sins left to church and family, which implies legal drugs; some adherents stress moral disapproval.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Law is confined to prohibiting force, theft and fraud, so speech restrictions have no place; Christian libertarianism treats liberty of conscience and expression as basic.

strong-leader.rationale: Sandlin and Acton-style liberty stress limited, law-bound government and Christians may resist tyranny, so a leader bypassing checks is opposed.

state-harmful.rationale: Anarchist and minarchist strands exist; Sandlin gives the state a limited ministry of justice while Hübner is sympathetic to anarchism, so the typical adherent answers neither way.

limit-guns.rationale: Self-defence is responsive force, and libertarians resist state disarmament of peaceful people; no source discusses guns directly.

empower-police-military.rationale: The state's job is restraining evil in a narrow sphere and Hübner is strongly critical of war and state violence, so more power and funding is opposed.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Law is limited to coercion so it follows that consensual transactions are not criminal, though adherents condemn the practice morally and sources do not mention it.

decide-locally.rationale: Hübner lists decentralization and diffusion of power as a libertarian principle, favouring local over national authority.

rehabilitation.rationale: Sandlin sees the state's role as punishing evildoers and restraining evil, with restitution; sources do not address rehabilitation versus punishment.

traditional-family.rationale: Sandlin places the family as a distinct God-given sphere with husband and wife roles and parental discipline of children.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Hübner says whether the state calls a contract marriage changes little, but views on legal recognition differ among Christian libertarians who also hold traditional views on marriage.

abortion-legal.rationale: Sandlin treats abortion as murder the state should suppress and Hübner counts it among wrongs, but libertarian Christians disagree and some prefer non-legal remedies.

more-religion-public.rationale: Sandlin wants society Christianized by family and church, not by the state, so a larger public role through state action is rejected, yet public religious influence is welcomed.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Hübner opposes racism and state injustices, but state programmes of correction require taxation and coercion that adherents resist; voluntary action preferred.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Sandlin affirms God-given roles in marriage; sources do not discuss the social construction of gender.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Libertarian principles are indifferent to nationality and the sources do not discuss national culture.

gradual-change.rationale: Sources give no position on pace of social change; adherents want liberty widened but not through revolution.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Hübner rejects the state as border-enforcing aggressor and libertarians favour free movement, but Christian libertarians differ and sources do not address it.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Supranational bodies concentrate coercive power, against the decentralization principle and the rule that the state is held to non-aggression.

free-trade.rationale: Sandlin gives the state no mandate over the economy, and Hübner praises free exchange, so trade restrictions are rejected.

nation-first.rationale: Libertarian emphasis on the individual and criticism of war rule out nationalist priority, though sources do not discuss it directly.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Hübner calls war mass murder and applies non-aggression to the state, so military intervention abroad is not justified.

open-borders.rationale: Non-aggression and freedom of movement point to open borders, but Christian libertarians differ and no source states it.

limit-growth.rationale: Voluntary market growth is welcome and state limits are coercive; sources do not discuss environmental limits.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Drastic government action means taxation and regulation beyond the magistrate's biblical sphere; harm to others would be dealt with by liability.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Hübner notes market innovation and charity platforms, but no source asserts that technology will solve most problems.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; adherents favour markets over subsidy and would not take a stand on energy mix.

revolution-justified.rationale: Sandlin says Christians may resist tyranny but may not lead revolutions, so revolution is not endorsed as a normal means.

experts-over-public.rationale: Hübner criticizes state bureaucratic committees insulated from consumers and prizes individual choice over rule by officials.

central-planning.rationale: Sandlin says Scripture gives the state no warrant to regulate the economy beyond honest weights and measures, which excludes planning.

socialized-markets.rationale: Voluntary worker or public ownership would be permitted but state-owned arrangements rely on coercion; sources do not discuss this formula.

land-value-tax.rationale: Sandlin forbids taxation for welfare and other purposes beyond restraining evil; a replacement land tax is not discussed and still taxes.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Heavy inheritance taxes are redistributive taxation which Sandlin says the state cannot warrant, and they fall on family property.

basic-income.rationale: Sandlin says the state may not tax to fund welfare and has no task of redistributing wealth; an unconditional state income is exactly that.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Tariffs are state economic regulation outside the biblical sphere and an interference in voluntary exchange.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Sandlin allows no state direction of the economy beyond honest weights and measures.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Wide ownership is welcome but adherents oppose state action to engineer it; sources do not address it.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Voluntary exchange and contract are central, and Hübner defends free markets as the human order of cooperation.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Hübner calls the Federal Reserve a monopolised currency funding fraud and creating poverty, and the Ron Paul wing opposes it.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognised bodies setting wages and prices are state economic regulation that Sandlin excludes.

one-party-rule.rationale: Limited, law-bound government and liberty as guardian of religious liberty exclude rule by a single party.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Christian libertarians draw on thinkers like Lord Acton but sources say nothing about hereditary monarchy; limited constitutional forms would be tolerated.

democracy-best.rationale: Sources do not rank forms of government; adherents tend to distrust majoritarian democracy that overrides rights.

direct-votes.rationale: Sources do not address direct democracy; adherents care about limiting what any majority may do.

workers-councils.rationale: Councils as the basis of political power conflicts with limited government and Sandlin's separate spheres of authority.

right-to-secede.rationale: Hübner stresses decentralization and the diffusion of power, and libertarians accept voluntary withdrawal from the state.

natural-rulers.rationale: Christian libertarianism builds on equal God-given rights and individual liberty, so a natural ruling class is rejected.

political-violence-never.rationale: Hübner is strongly nonviolent while Sandlin allows resistance to tyranny but not leading revolution; adherents differ on the absolute.

war-builds-character.rationale: Hübner calls war mass murder and says libertarian perspectives on peace do not search for exceptions to nonviolence.

separate-church-state.rationale: Sandlin gives church and state distinct jurisdictions and Hübner notes the harm of Christianity's marriage with the state in the 300s.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Sandlin holds that the state should enforce only what Scripture explicitly assigns it, which is narrower than basing laws on scripture generally; strands differ on theonomy.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Anarcho-capitalist-leaning thinkers discussed by Hübner favour it while others accept a minimal state with courts; adherents are not agreed.

military-superiority.rationale: Hübner holds war to be mass murder and criticises empire; maintaining superiority over rivals runs against this.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Equal God-given individual rights and the individualist tradition exclude ethnic definitions of the nation.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Hübner stresses voluntary cooperation and the state as oppressor, not class conflict as history's engine.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Sandlin denies the state any redistributive role, and liberty under law implies equality before the law, not of outcomes.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Property claims are respected and eminent domain opposed, but sources do not discuss indigenous authority.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Hübner opposes taxation-funded transfers and holds individuals responsible for their own acts; sources do not discuss reparations.

civilizational-union.rationale: Political union across states enlarges state power against decentralization; sources do not mention it.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Christian libertarians defend freedom but Hübner rejects the charge of selfishness and holds that liberty presupposes social bonds and charity.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Christian libertarianism stresses God-given inalienable individual rights, though under God's law and moral duties; rights come first against the community.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Sources do not address environmental ethics; Christian creation theology might support some value in nature.

limit-population.rationale: Coercive population limits violate non-aggression and Christians generally affirm children.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Hübner praises the markets' marvels and improvements of civilisation.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Markets that accommodate rapid change are praised, but no source endorses accelerating disruption as a goal.

human-enhancement.rationale: Individual liberty would allow it, but Christian views on human nature give adherents moral reservations; sources do not address it.

algorithmic-government.rationale: More state decision-making of any kind runs against limited government, whoever or whatever makes the decisions.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Hübner treats state intrusion as aggression, so private citizens may protect their communications.

restore-past-order.rationale: Sandlin looks to biblical law rather than to a lost social order; sources do not state this.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Sandlin judges policy by God's law, a principled test rather than a results test.

direct-action.rationale: Sandlin says Christians resist tyranny but should not lead revolutions; political change is sought mostly by persuasion, church and family.

means-match-ends.rationale: Hübner insists on nonviolence and voluntary means in building a free society, so methods are meant to reflect the end.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Hübner celebrates the unending marvels and improvements of market civilisation and rejects primitivism.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Market exchange between specialised producers is the core of the free order he defends.

distribute-by-need.rationale: State redistribution is outside the magistrate's remit, and voluntary charity is not a rule of distribution.

production-for-use.rationale: Profit and loss in free markets are defended as the reward for serving consumers.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Profit is treated as the reward for better goods and services under consumer sovereignty, not exploitation.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Hübner calls the state the overt oppressing class and holds all coercive power to non-aggression.

collective-farming.rationale: Forced collectivisation violates property and non-aggression; voluntary communities are allowed.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Hübner blames states and empire, not markets, for war.

taxation-theft.rationale: Hübner quotes the view that taxation is theft and asks when Christians may refuse to pay; Sandlin allows limited taxes so adherents differ in degree.

harm-principle.rationale: Law is limited to assault, theft and fraud, and other sins are for the church; Sandlin allows some biblically specified crimes beyond harm, such as idolatry.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Christian libertarianism rests on inalienable God-given individual rights, though the family and church are recognised spheres.

conscription.rationale: Hübner holds the state to the non-aggression principle, so forced service is aggression, and cites early Christian refusal of military service.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Libertarians value the freedom to leave and decentralization, but the sources do not rank it against voting.

state-as-business.rationale: Hübner says consumers can't withhold payment from the state, wanting more exit, but not that governments should be run as businesses.

positive-liberty.rationale: Liberty is non-interference and non-aggression; entitlement to means would require taxation.

media-academia-power.rationale: Hübner criticises public schooling and universities as indoctrinating but the sources don't compare their power to elected officials.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Hübner opposes racism and holds equal dignity before God, but sources do not address genetics.

organic-representation.rationale: Hübner values decentralization and voluntary association but no source proposes family and trade representation in place of parties.

total-state.rationale: Sandlin says the state is a limited ministry of justice that restrains evil and may not run education, health or the economy.

national-rebirth.rationale: Sandlin wants cultural renewal by church and family, not a state-led national rebirth; sources do not use this idea.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Hübner counts war and eminent domain as mass murder and land theft under non-aggression.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority rests on law and voluntary contract, not personal oaths of lords.

bound-labor.rationale: Hübner names forced labour and forced sharing as immoral and as violations of non-aggression.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Sandlin's Reformed outlook holds that God's law is a universal standard, against relativism, though presuppositionalists stress that no thought is neutral.

universal-morality.rationale: Sandlin rests civil limits on God's law, a universal standard, and natural rights are God-given.

single-common-good.rationale: Individualist libertarianism treats politics as protecting rights rather than pursuing a single common good.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Sources do not address Zionism; Christian libertarians differ because of dispensationalist views and opposition to foreign aid and war.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Not addressed; libertarians accept free movement but adherents reject state citizenship schemes.

revive-national-language.rationale: State language policy is coercive and outside the narrow state role; sources do not discuss it.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Democratic control rights imposed by law violate property and contract; firms may choose such structures voluntarily.

school-vouchers.rationale: Sandlin opposes taxing for education, so state vouchers still rely on taxation, though many libertarians accept them as a step to markets.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Hübner opposes the state's fiat money and Federal Reserve and Sandlin allows no economic management, so stimulus spending is rejected.

economic-freedom.rationale: Lord Acton, cited as a figure, tied political liberty to religious liberty, and Hübner defends economic freedom with civil freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: Sandlin says the state restrains evil rather than making men good, but also holds moral renewal belongs to church and family; no statement about rulers' example.

national-self-determination.rationale: Decentralisation and voluntary association support self-government, but the sources do not address nations specifically.

force-without-un.rationale: Hübner opposes war as mass murder, so any unapproved use of force abroad is worse.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Sandlin grounds his argument in Scripture and God's law, and the ideology is Christian by definition.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare itself is rejected as a state function, so the question of its eligibility does not arise.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Welfare is rejected as a state function; Christian charity may set work conditions, but no source addresses it.

class-collaboration.rationale: Hübner stresses voluntary social cooperation and peaceful exchange between people, though not in corporatist terms.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Property and inherited institutions are protected; the statement is destructive of them.

dominated-front.rationale: Hübner is hostile to blocs of states and to war, and the sources frame conflict as a matter of states, not of dominated nations organising against the West.

workers-nation.rationale: The sources treat individuals, not classes or nations, as the units of politics, so organising workers as a national class is not an aim.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Sandlin holds distinct roles in marriage and family but not in law, as the state may not enforce them in public life.

ban-interest.rationale: Voluntary lending contracts are protected exchange and Sandlin allows no economic regulation beyond honest weights and measures.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Hübner names forced education and coercive social dynamics as wrong and defends equal rights; state classification by race is state coercion.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Hübner, following Oppenheimer and Rothbard, calls the state the overt oppressing class, though this is Rothbardian and not Sandlin's view.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Sandlin gives the state no economic role, so state limits on production would lack warrant; the sources never mention energy.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Forced assimilation is state coercion, though the sources never discuss immigrants and adherents may expect assimilation socially.

elite-replacement.rationale: Hübner opposes racism and collective blame, and a plot theory of this kind has no basis in the Christian libertarian sources.

proportional-representation.rationale: The sources discuss limits on power, not electoral systems, and adherents have no common view on seat allocation.

national-mission.rationale: Hübner's rejection of empire and aggressive war excludes a mission to spread a form of government to other peoples.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Sandlin holds that husband and wife have different roles under God and does not see a structure of male advantage; the sources do not address it directly.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Hübner stresses that politicians need only satisfy a few wealthy people and criticises state institutions, though he does not use the phrasing about being out of touch.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Forced limits on who may have children are aggression against persons, which Hübner says binds the state like anyone else.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Hübner holds that the state has no second morality, so officials who torture or kill are accountable like private offenders.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Law is limited to prohibiting assault, theft and fraud; Sandlin accepts a ministry of justice but also some biblical crimes beyond it.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Hübner defends individual freedom in marriage and contract and opposes racism; state discouragement is coercion.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Inalienable God-given rights and Hübner's equality before God make equal worth and equal rights basic.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Marxist doctrine of no relevance to the ideology; adherents are opposed to socialism in any case.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Sources do not address this; adherents respect property claims and oppose state-driven displacement.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Equality before the law is implied but sources do not address religious personal law.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Forced worship is cited by Hübner as an offence against liberty, and Sandlin says refusing baptism is not for the state to punish.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: The state should not criminalise peaceful use of property; sources do not address it.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Sandlin denies the state a role in education and Hübner criticises forced education; religious instruction by the state would be coercive.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Hübner opposes any growth of state power, holding the state to non-aggression.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Voluntary relationships are the model Hübner defends; coercion without consent is the wrong libertarians oppose.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist targets are state manipulation of trade; adherents favour free exchange.

population-transfer.rationale: Forced movement of people is aggression, which Hübner says is wrong whoever commits it, including the state.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Hübner states the non-aggression principle as the core: initiating force is wrong and the state is not exempt.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Hübner praises market competition for improvement but rejects struggle between peoples; the statement bundles both.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Law is limited to prohibiting assault, theft and fraud, so banning parties for their ideas is outside it.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Sources treat liberty as non-aggression; arbitrary power matters but the concept is republican, not discussed.

separated-powers.rationale: Hübner stresses decentralization and diffusion of power as a libertarian principle.

vanguard-party.rationale: Hübner rejects hierarchical coercion and the state as oppressing class, and favours voluntary persuasion.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Hübner values care for the poor but through personal charity, not institutional priority in law.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Not addressed; adherents favour private ownership but oppose state housing in the first place.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Voluntary association and contract support the right to strike; peaceful picketing is not aggression, but force would be.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Hübner blames state policy and monopolised money for poverty, not population growth.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Hübner opposes racism and favours voluntary association among all kinds of people; the sources do not address social cohesion.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Not addressed; adherents would limit the offices rather than reform their filling.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Hübner says non-aggression binds the state, with no second moral standard for governments, and rejects torture and war exceptions.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Sandlin allows no state economic regulation beyond honest weights and measures.

party-controls-media.rationale: Law is limited to assault, theft and fraud and liberty of conscience is central, so state control of media is excluded.

party-commands-army.rationale: Hübner opposes the state's military violence; a party army multiplies state power.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Not addressed; adherents who reject state citizenship control differ from those who accept border rules.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Not addressed; adherents favour smaller government but sources do not speak of pay.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Not addressed by the sources and not an issue for the ideology.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Hübner favours decentralization over central powers; a supranational union concentrates it.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Sandlin allows a ministry of justice, but no source discusses the command structure.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Sandlin separates church jurisdiction from the state and the state has no say in church governance; denominations differ.

clerical-rule.rationale: Sandlin gives church and state separate jurisdictions and denies the state the power to make men good.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Hübner opposes war as mass murder but does not advocate working for defeat.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Other sins are for church and family and not law, so censorship for virtue is outside the legal sphere.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Not addressed; limited government outlook favours checks on rulers.

recall-officials.rationale: Hübner favours constraints on those holding power; recall is not discussed in the sources.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Hübner cites Ron Paul's opposition to an empire needing aggressive wars; non-entanglement follows.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Contract and property rights are protected and the state may not forbid voluntary exchange.

people-in-arms.rationale: Hübner opposes standing war power but sources do not discuss militias.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The sources do not compare rural and urban life, and there is nothing in the principles to decide it.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Not addressed; adherents would emphasise self-determination and oppose war to achieve it.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Hübner criticises public universities but the sources do not state this.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Biblical standards judge cultural practice, so cultures are not all equal; sources do not discuss.

death-penalty.rationale: Sandlin names murder as a crime for the state to punish, but sources do not discuss capital punishment; adherents differ, some citing the early church.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Sandlin denies the state a role in education and holds children under parental discipline and instruction.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Sandlin opposes state education altogether, so teaching creationism in state schools is not sought by statute.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Law is limited to assault, theft and fraud, with other sins for church and family; Sandlin does not list pornography as a state matter.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The sources say nothing on nationality law, and libertarian principles do not settle descent against birthplace.

minority-language-support.rationale: State funding of services violates the limit on taxation; private provision is allowed.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Religious liberty is the essential value Acton ties to political liberty, but exemptions are less relevant where laws are minimal.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Hübner values freedom to live differently and criticises coerced conformity, though not citing Mill.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Not addressed; adherents oppose state lending and aid but also coercive collection by arms.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Not addressed; adherents emphasise free markets as the basis of freedom.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The sources discuss limits on government, not how constitutions are drafted, so adherents have no common view.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Political liberty is held to be essential guardian of religious liberty and no trade of freedom for growth is acceptable.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Private charity is encouraged but state aid funded by taxation has no biblical warrant, so a duty exists for individuals, not governments; the statement is about countries.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Hübner opposes war and empire, though deterrence is not discussed.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The sources do not discuss how an executive is chosen; the ideology concerns what any office may do.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Hübner opposes the central bank as a monopolised, fraud-funding currency.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial settlements are not discussed; adherents favour peace and oppose war but also respect property claims.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Property is a right protected against theft and eminent domain, not a conditional privilege.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Soviet classification is a Marxist-tradition debate not taken up by the Christian libertarian sources.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Pre-emptive regulation goes beyond the limited sphere; harms are for liability after the fact.

collective-defense.rationale: Hübner's opposition to war and empire runs against automatic alliance obligations.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Hübner calls war and land seizure aggression, so annexation without consent is unlawful by the same standard.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Sandlin gives church its own jurisdiction beyond the state's reach.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The sources do not discuss ceremonial heads of state, and the principles do not decide it.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Hübner counts war as mass murder and supports decentralization, so force against secession is aggression.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Decentralisation and diffusion of power are advocated.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Sandlin says the state is a limited ministry bound by God's law, with no sacred status for rulers.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Sandlin opposes taxation beyond the narrow state functions, so adherents prefer less tax to flat tax; the sources do not discuss the form.

character-from-environment.rationale: Christian doctrine holds fallen human nature, but upbringing matters too; Sandlin places discipline in family.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Sandlin holds that God's law limits all human authority and the state may do only what Scripture assigns it.

space-expansion.rationale: Space policy is not discussed; adherents would not fund it by taxation but would allow private ventures.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical mixed constitutions are not discussed; Hübner values diffused power but offers no constitutional form.

leader-cult.rationale: Idolatry is condemned in Christian doctrine, and Sandlin treats rulers as bound under God's law rather than as objects of mass praise.

equal-parenting.rationale: Custody rules are not discussed; contract and parental rights pull in different directions for adherents.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist doctrine outside the Christian libertarian sources, which reject socialism altogether.

land-redistribution.rationale: Hübner calls eminent domain land theft; the state taking land and giving it to others is theft.

refugee-return.rationale: The sources do not discuss refugees; property rights favour return but sources do not apply them.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Hübner holds the state to non-aggression and calls war and territorial seizure wrong.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Sandlin says the state cannot punish refusing baptism and the church disciplines only by its own means; forced worship is condemned by Hübner.

women-must-cover.rationale: Law is limited to assault, theft and fraud, so dress codes are not legal matters.

common-currency.rationale: Hübner opposes monopolised state currency; a shared state currency extends it.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Unions of kin peoples enlarge state power and the sources centre on individuals; they do not discuss the idea.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority self-government of this kind is not discussed; adherents favour decentralisation but through voluntary association.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The sources centre on individual rights everywhere but do not discuss minority emigration versus staying.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Christian libertarians ground social order in God's law and moral choice, not in economic determinism.

ban-cartels.rationale: Sandlin opposes state economic regulation, and cartels backed by state privilege would be opposed; voluntary ones are not seen as a state matter.

no-bailouts.rationale: Hübner links Federal Reserve fraud to poverty, and Sandlin allows no state economic role, so bailouts are condemned.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Liberty is a guard against majority power, so courts should limit what a majority may choose.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: State quotas are coercive and outside the narrow state role.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarkic blocs mean trade controls the state may not impose.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Binding standards in trade are state economic regulation beyond Sandlin's limits.

moral-incentives.rationale: Voluntary exchange and market incentives are defended; compulsory duty replaces them.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Sandlin says Christians may not lead revolutions and Hübner's nonviolence rejects armed vanguards.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Special legal privileges are state coercion; liberty under equal law excludes inherited legal privilege, though private inheritance remains.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Curriculum content is not discussed; Sandlin removes the state from schooling in any case.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Hübner holds non-aggression binds the state and forbids one people's rule over another by force.

patriotic-education.rationale: Sandlin denies the state a role in education.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Hübner opposes state coercion and legal privilege, so racial preferences by law would be rejected.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Crisis theory is not discussed; Hübner defends markets as adaptive but does not address collapse.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Hübner's opposition to empire excludes cultivated influence by state power.

delink-world-market.rationale: Hübner defends free exchange but also criticises state power; the statement concerns state policy of delinking.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Not addressed; adherents reject exploitation theories.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Hübner's freedom of contract and association applies to any partners, though adherents condemn such discrimination morally.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Inalienable God-given rights are central and limits on the state are sought.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Hübner opposes imperial seizure, but the sources do not discuss the force of colonial treaties.

elective-rulers.rationale: Consent and limited rule favour election over inheritance, though sources do not rank forms.

minority-veto.rationale: Hübner values voluntary consent but sources do not say that a single dissenter can block decisions; anarchist strands do, minarchist ones do not.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Sandlin says Christians may resist civil tyranny, though not lead revolutions.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Liberty is a limit on every authority, parliament included.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The sources do not discuss animals; Christian views of creation allow both concern and use.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Hübner sees charity as a personal duty and stresses personal care for the poor, though not as noblesse oblige.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Sandlin wants Christianising of society through family and church, which is a withdrawal from state power but not from public life.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: A Frankfurt School claim not taken up by the sources, which see state schooling as the main shaper.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramscian hegemony is not discussed; Hübner stresses the state's use of coercion and indoctrination in public schooling.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Hübner blames states, monopolised money and war rather than world markets.

native-born-offices.rationale: Equal inalienable rights favour open access to office, though the sources do not discuss birthplace requirements.

party-own-road.rationale: Communist party relations are not part of the Christian libertarian sources.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: State aid is outside the state's mandate and Hübner favours voluntary charity and market development.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Hübner holds war to be mass murder, so war to regain land is wrong.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Equal rights and rejection of group political privilege exclude rule by descent.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Constitutional founding values are not discussed; adherents oppose fascism as a state power but also want limits on state definitions of ideology.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Hübner holds all states to non-aggression, which condemns both; he does not make the comparison.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: The sources do not discuss the Civil War, and adherents differ on this historical dispute.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Monuments are not discussed; adherents oppose state tax funding of both but have no common view.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: State programmes are outside the sphere; the sources do not discuss gender gaps in outcomes.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Assault is a crime whoever commits it, but the sources do not discuss services or relative seriousness.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: God's law is held as universal, so forms of limits on the state are not culture-bound.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Hübner holds war and state force to non-aggression and opposes military power.

paid-care-work.rationale: State payment is taxation for a non-state purpose; Sandlin gives family a separate sphere.

filial-duty.rationale: Christian ethics of honouring parents, with family and church the care providers instead of the state; Sandlin does not discuss it explicitly.

office-by-exam.rationale: Civil service recruitment is not discussed; adherents would shrink the state rather than reform hiring.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: State economic control forbidden; voluntary sales are exchange.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Sandlin treats marriage vows as binding but sources do not state the legal rule; adherents differ.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Binding mandates are not discussed in the sources; they concern limits on power rather than delegate rules.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Hübner favours private provision over state pay-as-you-go schemes; adherents typically prefer private savings, though state-managed accounts are criticised.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Hübner holds property as a basic right and calls eminent domain theft.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Constraints on rulers are favoured; sources do not discuss.

single-official-language.rationale: State language compulsion is coercion outside the legitimate sphere.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Property and contract rights apply regardless of nationality.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Liability for unintended outcomes is state coercion without aggression.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Hübner cites Christian critics of consumerism and the question of Christians using state currency, but does not endorse a conclusion; Christians typically agree moral critique is legitimate while rejecting state remedy.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Hübner counts war and state violence as aggression; covert war is the same.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Invading an allied country is war, mass murder in Hübner's terms.

corporate-influence.rationale: Hübner opposes state privileges that lobbying seeks but not by campaign limits; it is a matter of the state's powers.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Voluntary gifts are exchange; restriction would be state coercion; sources do not discuss.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: State payments by taxation outside the limited sphere.

residents-only-property.rationale: Property transfers are voluntary exchange, and state limits violate property rights.

job-guarantee.rationale: Sandlin says the state may not tax for welfare nor redistribute wealth; an employer of last resort is both.

democratic-peace.rationale: Not addressed; Hübner opposes using war to spread anything.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Sandlin holds that God's law limits the state and allows resistance to tyranny but sources do not state that there is no general duty to obey; adherents differ on Romans 13.

non-intervention.rationale: Hübner applies non-aggression to the state and cites Ron Paul on empire requiring aggressive wars; he does not say literally for any reason.

industrial-unions.rationale: Union structure is not discussed, and voluntary organisation by any form would be permitted.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Hübner opposes racism and collective guilt, and an ethnic conspiracy theory has no place.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Hübner says what the state calls marriage changes little about the contract; Christian libertarians differ on whether to remove the state from marriage.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Not addressed; adherents want state accountability but sources do not state a legal right.

local-production.rationale: Voluntary choice, not mandate, is the model; sources do not discuss.

informal-organisation.rationale: Forms of political organisation are not discussed; Christian libertarians use church, family and voluntary groups but no specific model.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Not addressed; adherents distrust both supranational bodies and national power.

religious-nation.rationale: Sandlin separates church and state and denies that the state Christianises society.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Tribute to a power is incompatible with non-aggression and opposition to empire.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Decentralisation favours local retention; no source states it.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Not addressed; the ideology holds all property private.

defeat-communism.rationale: Hübner opposes socialism and communism, but opposes war to defeat them.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Hübner favours markets over state services; this mix still leaves public funding by taxation.

religion-illusion.rationale: Sandlin's argument is Christian in premise, and God's law is the basis of political limits.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Hübner praises the market's unending improvements of civilisation.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Hübner defends free markets and treats legal equality as sufficient.

socialized-care.rationale: Sandlin assigns welfare and children to family and church, not the state.

purge-loanwords.rationale: State language engineering is coercion beyond the legitimate sphere.

treaties-binding.rationale: Contracts should be kept and honoured; sources do not discuss treaties with nations.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Voluntary communities are allowed, but no source proposes society be reorganised that way.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Hübner defends free markets and criticises democratic socialism, so no third way.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Historic or religious claims are not discussed; property by first appropriation and contract points to present owners.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Hübner opposes state mass murder and the ideology stands against collective violence; sources do not discuss denial.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Law is limited to assault, theft and fraud, other sins for church and family, and Hübner defends freedom of contract between consenting partners.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Political liberty is the guardian of religious liberty and law punishes only force, theft and fraud.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Sandlin says idolatry may be punished by the state because Scripture assigns it, but most Christian libertarians hold other sins to be church matters; the typical adherent leans against.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Hübner holds state aggression and empire to be wrong.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: An Islamic doctrine not addressed by the Christian libertarian sources.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Sandlin limits resistance to tyranny and rejects leading revolutions, and Christians do not claim force against secular rulers for irreligion.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Not addressed; adherents favour decentralisation but not state-run participation.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Not addressed; adherents hold individual rights and see the state as chief oppressor.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Sandlin holds traditional views, though state legal recognition is a contract matter on which sources are silent.

assisted-dying.rationale: Not addressed; adherents differ between voluntary freedom and the sanctity of life.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Hübner cites libertarianism as distinct, though libertarians commonly say they transcend left-right; no source says it.

alienated-labor.rationale: Hübner defends voluntary work and market exchange as the humane order.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Not addressed; libertarian principles favour religious liberty.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Sandlin holds that God's law limits and defines legitimate civil authority and God-given rights ground liberty.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: State schools are rejected; individual freedom to dress is protected, but state employees' dress is not discussed.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Contract freedom is valued but fraud and force are crimes; sources do not discuss.

social-market-economy.rationale: Sandlin allows no state economic regulation or welfare funded by tax.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Hübner opposes war but a minimal state may keep defence, depending on the strand.

rich-first.rationale: Gradual development is not discussed; markets let some gain first but adherents have no stance on the phrasing.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Hübner cites Ron Paul on avoiding empire and entangling wars.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Hereditary leaders are not discussed; limited government makes succession matter less.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Voluntary mutual banks are allowed but no source favours them; Hübner opposes state-privileged credit.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: IMF conditions are not discussed; adherents favour fiscal restraint but oppose international lenders' power.

property-franchise.rationale: Inalienable rights belong to all individuals, which excludes franchise by property.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Not addressed; adherents hold that domination comes from the state.

reification.rationale: Hübner defends markets as voluntary relations between persons.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Property rights in presses and halls are protected.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Limited law under God's law implies rulers bound by known standing rules, though sources don't use this wording.

racial-franchise.rationale: Inalienable God-given rights belong to every individual.

online-participation.rationale: Digital deliberation is not discussed; adherents prefer limiting political decisions to expanding them.

open-government-data.rationale: Hübner holds the state to the same standards as anyone and opposes secrecy in war, though not explicitly.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Sandlin leaves marriage to family and church, and Hübner defends freedom of contract.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Boycotts are voluntary but hostile to minority groups; Christian libertarians reject collective blame, so the typical adherent would not endorse.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Sortition forums are not discussed in the sources, and adherents want fewer public decisions overall.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Sandlin follows Scripture as authority, not reinterpretation for modern conditions.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Hübner locates the threat to liberty in state power, not in wealth earned in the market, though concentrated wealth tied to state power is condemned.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Hübner opposes the military, and individual freedom favours inclusion but sources do not address it.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Sandlin denies the state a role in education and Christians reject state atheism.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Sandlin holds that the state's justice ministry punishes evildoers, though anarchist strands would provide justice privately.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Consociational government is not discussed; Hübner favours decentralisation but offers no model.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Sandlin says welfare belongs to church, family and private associations, not the state, and Hübner says the poor need personal charity.

term-limits.rationale: Constraints on political power are valued; sources do not mention terms.

vote-delegation.rationale: Liquid democracy is not discussed in the sources.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Not addressed; priorities for state policy are limited.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Hübner takes up egalitarian and complementarian views as divisive issues within Christian libertarians.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Hübner notes the egalitarian debate is divisive and Sandlin teaches husband authority; adherents differ by denomination.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Voting rights of foreign residents are not discussed; adherents distrust expanding state decision-making.

rent-control.rationale: Sandlin permits no state regulation of the economy beyond honest weights and measures.

abolish-ip.rationale: Sandlin counts copyright infringement as theft, while Hübner notes the debate with Kinsella against IP; adherents differ.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Hübner condemns forced education and forced worship, and state youth drilling is coerced collectivism.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Not addressed; opposition to war but silent on basing.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Hübner cites Ron Paul against an empire needing aggressive wars; bases are part of that empire.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Official recognition is not discussed, though Hübner condemns mass killing by states.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Returns to owning property are legitimate exchange; sources do not state it.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Hübner says force is legitimate when responsive, not an initiation of force; self-defence is not wrong.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: National origin myths are not discussed; the sources centre on individuals and not nations.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Sandlin affirms God-given roles and sources do not discuss the construction of sex.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Feminist theory is not discussed; Hübner mentions egalitarian and complementarian disputes only.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: National sainthood conflicts with the view that war is mass murder, but sources do not discuss martyrs.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Sandlin's Christian framework treats politics as moral under God, though he also stresses the state's narrow job.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Diaspora politics is not discussed in the sources.

culture-before-state.rationale: Sandlin says Christianising society is the role of family and church, not the state, so culture comes before state action.

god-not-male.rationale: Not addressed; Christian libertarians differ across denominations.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Sandlin treats Scripture as the authority which judges, not as judged.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Property and exchange belong to whoever owns and trades; state favour is aggression.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Administrative boundaries are not discussed; decentralisation would permit this voluntarily.

independent-unions.rationale: Voluntary associations independent of the state fit; sources do not address unions.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Hübner is critical of state services, though local provision is nearer his ideal than national; still taxation-funded.

second-chamber.rationale: Bicameralism is not discussed, though diffused power in general is favoured.

municipal-property.rationale: Property belongs to private owners rather than the community.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Hübner favours decentralisation and diffusion of power, but sources do not propose confederations.

family-wage.rationale: Wage levels are set by exchange, and the state may not regulate the economy; family wage as law is excluded.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Adherents oppose state regulation, which would mean faster approval; no source addresses it.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Tax-funded research has no warrant in the state's limited sphere.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Hübner treats state monopoly money and tracking as intrusion and adherents prize financial privacy.

online-anonymity.rationale: The state is held to the standard of non-aggression and privacy against its intrusion is protected.

person-over-state.rationale: Inalienable God-given individual rights make the state serve the person, and persons are not mere means.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The ideology is Christian and gives human beings a spiritual nature with God-given dignity.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Hübner favours decentralisation of power, so revocable powers go against it.

gm-crops.rationale: Adherents oppose state restrictions on voluntary innovation; no source discusses it.

dense-cities.rationale: Urban form is not discussed; adherents would leave it to markets and property owners.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Hübner stresses individuals, not groups, and opposes racism.

racial-pride.rationale: Not addressed; individualism and Christian humility pull both ways.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Hübner holds force to be legitimate only in response, never initiating, so defensive wars only.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Not addressed; the individual, not the nation, is the unit.

communal-electorates.rationale: Equal individual rights exclude group-based voting arrangements.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Not addressed; adherents do not read politics through foreign plots.

free-public-college.rationale: Sandlin says the state may not tax to fund education.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Taxes fall outside the narrow tax base; harm to property is addressed by liability, not taxes.

future-generations.rationale: Stewardship of creation is a Christian theme, but the sources don't address it; adherents would say through property and liability.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Difference feminism is not discussed in the sources; Hübner treats gender roles as a divisive topic.

arms-reduction.rationale: Hübner is critical of war and military power.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Hübner holds states to ordinary moral standards, but secrecy is not discussed.

capital-controls.rationale: State economic control beyond honest weights and measures is excluded.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The state is held to the same standards, and a monopoly on arms is a state privilege libertarians reject.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Hübner cites early Christian refusal of military service and calls war mass murder.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Voluntary bargaining is permitted but individual contract is the default; sources don't discuss it.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Topping up incomes is the redistribution Sandlin denies the state.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Limits on state borrowing fit the aim to constrain state power.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: State-managed restructuring of the world economy is regulation outside the state's sphere.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Anarchist strands might agree but Sandlin and Hübner favour peaceful means and no source calls for smashing.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Hübner's decentralisation lets communities choose their own arrangements.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Natural capital accounting is not discussed; property rights in resources are defended.

sacred-nation.rationale: Idolatry is condemned and Sandlin gives the state only a limited ministry of justice.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Sandlin says the state may not tax to fund education, so relieving debts by tax is excluded.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Regional exploitation theory is not discussed, though Hübner criticises central power over the periphery.

shared-human-nature.rationale: The ideology builds on God-given human nature and inalienable rights.

public-service-media.rationale: Tax-funded media is outside the narrow state role.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Christianity holds exclusive truth claims; Sandlin's argument rests on Scripture.

farm-price-support.rationale: Sandlin allows no state regulation of the economy beyond honest weights and measures, so price guarantees are excluded.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Hübner opposes war but sources do not address deterrence.

workers-own-party.rationale: Labour party politics is not discussed; adherents favour limited government over any class party.

ban-fgm.rationale: Mutilating a person is assault, which law properly punishes; consent of the child does not exist.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Equal inalienable rights and property rights apply to all individuals.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Linguistic classification is not discussed in the sources.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Harm to others' property is the aggression law addresses, so liability for proven harm is the libertarian remedy.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Not addressed; law is limited and rests on God's law rather than offices.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Liberty is held basic, with environmental harm addressed as harm to others.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Sandlin wants the state to punish evildoers but sources do not discuss sentencing.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: State requirements are coercive and not discussed.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Hübner holds forced association is a violation of liberty, applying to union membership.

voter-id.rationale: Election administration is not discussed in the sources and adherents have no common view.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Sandlin keeps the state from regulating religion, so no interpretation gets legal precedence.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Not addressed; adherents hold limits matter more than procedure.

premarital-sex.rationale: Christian sexual ethics disapproves, but Sandlin and Hübner treat it as a matter for church and family, not law.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Hübner holds state intrusion to the same standard of non-aggression as private acts.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Sandlin forbids taxing for welfare, so a state cash payment is still funded by tax; some libertarians accept it as a lesser evil.

women-suffrage.rationale: Inalienable rights belong to all individuals; Hübner notes the egalitarianism debate but legal equality of rights holds.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Sandlin affirms the biblical roles of husband and wife and the family as a God-given sphere.

race-social-construct.rationale: Hübner opposes racism but the sources do not discuss the scientific status of racial categories.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: State agencies funded by tax are outside the limited sphere.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Hübner draws on Rothbard-style property rights, and first appropriation by working unowned land is the account of Locke, whom the article lists among Christian libertarians.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Hübner holds leaders accountable for war crimes, but the sources show distrust of supranational bodies and do not discuss such courts.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Sandlin grounds the argument in Scripture as the authority, though not every adherent holds literalism.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Constitutional guarantees for Indigenous governance are not discussed in the sources.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Hübner opposes state economic control and holds the state to non-aggression.

indirect-election.rationale: Electoral procedure is not discussed; the ideology concerns limits on office rather than how it is filled.

national-church-status.rationale: Sandlin separates church and state, so a state church privilege has no place.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Decentralisation favoured, with no source on ethnic regions.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Consent and self-determination fit decentralist libertarianism; sources do not address it.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Border inheritance is not discussed, though war to redraw them is excluded.

simple-living.rationale: Not addressed; voluntary, so no policy stance.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: State restriction of purchases and residence is coercion.

equal-conscription.rationale: Hübner holds conscription to be aggression, so neither should be conscripted.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Spiritual ties to a land are not discussed; adherents emphasise individual property rather than national soil.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Killing without trial is initiating force and Hübner holds the state to non-aggression.

close-ties-china.rationale: Not addressed; adherents favour free trade and non-intervention.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Hübner opposes state military action abroad and expansion of state power.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Hübner defends private property in resources via first appropriation.

self-ownership.rationale: Free will and God-given inalienable rights over the person are the premise of the ideology.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Sandlin allows taxation only for narrow state functions, so cutting taxes is favoured.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Sandlin says welfare is not a state function at all, so targeted state spending is still excluded though less bad.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Hübner holds the state oppressive and rejects personalist rule.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Hübner criticises state favours and monopolies that distort the market and treats them as unjust.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Sandlin separates church and state and denies the state a Christianising role.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Hübner praises market innovation and Christians value tradition, but no source combines them as a programme.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Sandlin teaches that a wife vows to obey her husband, but women are free in law; sources do not discuss.

national-resource-control.rationale: Not addressed; private ownership is the aim.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Libertarian writing holds that property acquired and exchanged without force or fraud is just whatever the resulting inequality, and Sandlin ties the state's role to protecting such rights.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Inferred from Sandlin's limit on state taxation to its narrow functions; no source mentions this tax.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Inferred from the focus on individual responsibility and voluntary action over state remedies; the sources do not discuss race.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Sandlin holds that God's law limits all human authority, so a statute contradicting it lacks binding force.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Inferred as neutral: the sources say nothing on automation, and a market view neither pushes nor opposes it.

multipolar-world.rationale: Inferred from the critique of war and empire that follows from the state's ban on initiating force.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Inferred from the libertarian tradition, which usually favours subjective value; the sources do not address it.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: The sources do not address it; libertarian views split on patriotism and reject state-run worker politics.

material-over-identity.rationale: Not a left-right dispute the sources address; the profile has no position on it.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Inferred from the rejection of state direction of the economy; a party-led socialist system contradicts the core principles.

missingStatements.text: Conduct that harms no one else should be a matter for churches and families to address, not for the criminal law.
missingStatements.rationale: The Wikipedia article says law is limited to prohibiting assault, theft and fraud while other sins go to the church or parents, and Sandlin assigns moral discipline to church and family.

missingStatements.text: The state should do only what it is explicitly authorised to do, and it is bound by a higher law than its own.
missingStatements.rationale: Sandlin argues God's law limits all human authority so the state may do only what Scripture requires of it, and Hübner holds the state to the same moral rules as individuals.

notes: Adherents differ on whether any state is legitimate (minarchist versus anarchist strands), on abortion (most pro-life, some libertarian arguments for choice), on same-sex marriage law, and on immigration, so those answers are low confidence.
